blocks.text: Pufferfish (fugu) poisoning begins with tingling around the lips and ends with paralysis while the victim stays fully conscious. The toxin, tetrodotoxin, plugs one type of ion channel, and nerve impulses simply stop travelling. To see why, we need to understand how a neurone holds a voltage and then briefly throws it away.

blocks.markdown:
Every neurone is a leaky capacitor. The lipid bilayer separates two salt solutions, and a small excess of negative charge sits just inside the membrane. The resulting voltage difference (inside minus outside) is the **membrane potential**, $V_m$, measured in millivolts (mV). Two things set it: **concentration gradients** maintained by pumps, and **relative permeabilities** to each ion through leak channels.

The $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$-ATPase uses ATP to export 3 $\text{Na}^+$ and import 2 $\text{K}^+$ per cycle. This keeps $\text{K}^+$ high inside (about 140 mmol/L inside versus 4-5 mmol/L outside) and $\text{Na}^+$ high outside (about 145 mmol/L outside versus 10-15 mmol/L inside). Values vary a little between textbooks and cell types.

blocks.title: Equilibrium potential
blocks.text: The equilibrium potential $E_X$ of an ion X is the membrane voltage at which the electrical force on X exactly balances its concentration gradient, so there is no net flux of X. It depends only on the concentration ratio and the ion's valence.

blocks.caption: Nernst equation. R is the gas constant, T absolute temperature, z the valence, F Faraday's constant.

blocks.title: Potassium equilibrium potential
blocks.prompt: A motor neurone has $[\text{K}^+]_{out} = 4$ mmol/L and $[\text{K}^+]_{in} = 140$ mmol/L at 37 degrees C. Calculate $E_K$.

steps.text: Identify z for potassium: it is a monovalent cation, so $z = +1$.
Form the concentration ratio $[\text{K}^+]_{out}/[\text{K}^+]_{in} = 4/140 = 0.0286$, and take log base 10: $\log_{10}(0.0286) = -1.54$.

blocks.answer: $E_K \approx -95$ mV. The negative sign means the inside of the cell is negative at the point where outward K+ diffusion is balanced.

blocks.markdown:
In a resting neurone the membrane is far more permeable to $\text{K}^+$ than to $\text{Na}^+$ (many open K+ leak channels, very few open Na+ channels). The resting potential is therefore pulled close to $E_K$ but not quite there, because a small $\text{Na}^+$ leak drags it slightly positive. The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz idea is that $V_m$ is a permeability-weighted average of the equilibrium potentials. A typical resting value for a neurone is about -70 mV, with $E_{Na}$ about +60 mV.

The pump contributes little directly to the resting voltage. Its main job is to maintain the gradients over minutes to hours.

blocks.caption: Approximate values; they vary with cell type and temperature.

blocks.markdown:
An **action potential** is a brief, all-or-none, self-regenerating reversal of $V_m$ that travels along the axon. It is driven by two families of voltage-gated channels. **Voltage-gated $\text{Na}^+$ channels** have two gates: a fast activation gate that opens with depolarisation, and an inactivation gate that closes a millisecond later and then stays shut until the membrane repolarises. **Voltage-gated $\text{K}^+$ channels** are slower: they open with depolarisation and close slowly on repolarisation.

The phases are: (1) a stimulus depolarises the axon hillock to **threshold** (about -55 mV); (2) rapid **upstroke** as Na+ channels open and positive feedback drives $V_m$ toward $E_{Na}$; (3) **peak** at about +30 to +40 mV, short of $E_{Na}$ because inactivation has begun; (4) **repolarisation** as Na+ channels inactivate and K+ channels open; (5) **undershoot** (after-hyperpolarisation) while K+ channels remain open, driving $V_m$ close to $E_K$; (6) return to rest.

blocks.title: Why the nerve cannot fire again at once
blocks.prompt: Immediately after the peak of an action potential a second, very strong stimulus is applied. Explain why no second spike results.

steps.text: At the peak, the Na+ channels' inactivation gates have closed. Inactivated channels cannot open, however much the membrane is depolarised.
Inactivation is only removed when $V_m$ returns toward rest, so for a short time almost no Na+ channels are available. This is the absolute refractory period.
Later, during the undershoot, enough channels have recovered to fire, but open K+ channels hold $V_m$ near $E_K$, so a larger-than-normal stimulus is needed. This is the relative refractory period.

blocks.answer: The absolute refractory period reflects Na+ channel inactivation. It limits firing frequency and makes the impulse travel in one direction only, because the segment just behind the impulse is refractory.

items: Threshold: enough Na+ channels open that inward Na+ current exceeds outward K+ current, so depolarisation becomes self-reinforcing.
All-or-none: once threshold is reached the amplitude is fixed by channel properties, not stimulus strength.
Stimulus strength is coded by firing frequency and by the number of axons recruited.

blocks.markdown: **Propagation.** Local current spreads ahead of the active region and depolarises the next patch to threshold. In an **unmyelinated axon** this happens continuously along the whole length. Speed rises with axon diameter (lower internal resistance), so unmyelinated C fibres conduct at roughly 0.5-2 m/s. In a **myelinated axon**, oligodendrocytes (CNS) or Schwann cells (PNS) wrap the axon in insulating membrane that lowers capacitance and leak. Voltage-gated Na+ channels are clustered at gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**, and the impulse jumps from node to node: **saltatory conduction**. Large myelinated fibres conduct at up to about 70-120 m/s, and it is also more energy-efficient because less ion movement must be pumped back.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.text: The resting potential is not E_K and not E_Na; it is between them, closer to E_K. The action potential does not reach E_Na because Na+ channels inactivate and K+ channels open. And myelin does not make the axon conduct 'faster' by speeding channels up; it reduces capacitance and leak so that current reaches the next node sooner.

points: Resting potential is set by the K+ gradient and high resting K+ permeability, shifted slightly positive by a Na+ leak; the pump maintains the gradients.
The Nernst equation gives the equilibrium potential of one ion from its concentration ratio.
The action potential is an all-or-none event shaped by Na+ channel activation and inactivation and delayed K+ channel opening; inactivation causes the absolute refractory period.
Myelination and larger diameter increase conduction speed; saltatory conduction jumps between nodes of Ranvier.

questions.stem: Why is the resting membrane potential of a typical neurone (about -70 mV) less negative than the potassium equilibrium potential?

options.text: Because a small resting Na+ permeability pulls the membrane slightly toward E_Na
Because the Na+/K+-ATPase pumps more K+ out than it brings in
Because K+ channels are completely closed at rest
Because chloride is actively pumped into the cell

questions.correctOptionText: Because a small resting Na+ permeability pulls the membrane slightly toward E_Na

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Vm is a permeability-weighted average, so a small Na+ leak pulls it a little positive of E_K.
distractorRationale.b: The pump imports 2 K+ and exports 3 Na+; it does not export K+.
distractorRationale.c: K+ leak channels are open at rest; that is why Vm is near E_K.
distractorRationale.d: Chloride is not the main determinant and is not actively pumped into the neurone at rest.

questions.explanation: The resting potential is a weighted average of the equilibrium potentials, weighted by permeability. K+ permeability dominates, so Vm is close to E_K (about -90 mV), but the small Na+ leak, whose equilibrium potential is positive, shifts it to about -70 mV.

questions.stem: A cultured neurone is bathed in solution with [Na+] outside = 145 mmol/L and [Na+] inside = 12 mmol/L at 37 degrees C. Using E = (61.5 mV / z) log10(out/in), calculate the Na+ equilibrium potential in mV.
questions.explanation: Na+ has z = +1, so E_Na = 61.5 x log10(145/12). The ratio is 12.08 and its log10 is 1.082, giving about +66.5 mV. The positive sign shows that Na+ entry is favoured both by concentration and by the negative interior, which is why opening Na+ channels depolarises the cell.

questions.stem: During the absolute refractory period immediately after the peak of an action potential, a second spike cannot be triggered by any stimulus. Which channel state best explains this?

options.text: Voltage-gated K+ channels are all closed
Voltage-gated Na+ channels are in the inactivated state
The Na+/K+-ATPase has stopped working
Leak K+ channels have closed

questions.correctOptionText: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are in the inactivated state

distractorRationale.a: K+ channels are open at this stage; closed K+ channels would make firing easier.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: inactivated Na+ channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises.
distractorRationale.c: The pump is slow and not needed for individual spikes; its failure would not stop a single spike.

questions.explanation: After the upstroke the Na+ inactivation gates close, and they only reset once the membrane repolarises. Until enough channels have reset, no depolarisation can generate the regenerative Na+ current, so no spike occurs.

questions.stem: Which combination of channel events produces repolarisation of the axon after the peak of the action potential?

options.text: Na+ channel activation and K+ channel closure
Na+ channel inactivation and delayed opening of voltage-gated K+ channels
Opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels throughout the axon
Reversal of the Na+/K+-ATPase

questions.correctOptionText: Na+ channel inactivation and delayed opening of voltage-gated K+ channels

distractorRationale.a: That would continue depolarisation, not repolarise.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: stopping the inward Na+ current and adding outward K+ current brings Vm back down.
distractorRationale.c: Ca2+ channels are not responsible for axonal repolarisation.
distractorRationale.d: The pump does not reverse and is too slow to shape the spike.

questions.explanation: Repolarisation needs inward current to fall and outward current to rise. Na+ inactivation removes the inward current, while the slower voltage-gated K+ channels open and let K+ leave.

questions.stem: Explain why the membrane potential undershoots the resting value (after-hyperpolarisation) at the end of an action potential, and state one consequence for the next stimulus.
markingGuide: Voltage-gated K+ channels open with depolarisation and close more slowly than Na+ channels inactivate
K+ permeability is transiently higher than at rest
Vm therefore moves closer to E_K (about -90 mV) than the resting potential
Na+ channels are recovering from inactivation meanwhile
Consequence: relative refractory period, a larger stimulus is needed to reach threshold
questions.explanation: The voltage-gated K+ channels that opened during the spike close slowly, so for a few milliseconds K+ permeability exceeds its resting value and Vm is pulled toward E_K. The membrane is then further from threshold, so a supra-normal stimulus is needed, which defines the relative refractory period.

questions.stem: Saltatory conduction in a myelinated axon occurs because:

options.text: Action potentials are regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated
Myelin contains voltage-gated Na+ channels that fire in sequence
The axon membrane under myelin is more permeable to K+
Myelin actively pumps ions to speed depolarisation

questions.correctOptionText: Action potentials are regenerated only at nodes of Ranvier, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated

distractorRationale.a: Correct: current flows passively under the insulated segments and the spike is regenerated at the next node.
distractorRationale.b: Myelin is an insulating membrane, not a channel-bearing structure.
distractorRationale.c: Myelin reduces ion leakage; it does not increase K+ permeability.
distractorRationale.d: Myelin is passive insulation and does not pump ions.

questions.explanation: Myelin lowers capacitance and leak under each wrapped segment, so current passes quickly to the next node. Because Na+ channels are clustered at the nodes, the impulse is regenerated only there and appears to jump.

questions.stem: A myelinated sensory axon conducts at 50 m/s. How long, in milliseconds, does an impulse take to travel 0.8 m along it?
questions.explanation: Time = distance / speed = 0.8 m / 50 m/s = 0.016 s, which is 16 ms. For comparison, an unmyelinated fibre at 1 m/s would take 0.8 s over the same distance, showing the value of myelination.

questions.stem: True or false: a stronger depolarising stimulus above threshold produces an action potential of larger amplitude.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none: once threshold is reached the amplitude is set by channel properties and ion gradients. Stronger stimuli are coded by a higher firing frequency or by recruiting more axons.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing optic neuritis is found to have focal CNS demyelination. Which mechanism best explains slowed or blocked conduction along a demyelinated axon segment?

options.text: Na+ channels at the nodes are replaced by K+ channels
Increased capacitance and current leak mean less current reaches the next node, so it may fail to reach threshold
The resting potential becomes more negative, preventing depolarisation
The Na+/K+-ATPase becomes unable to maintain gradients

questions.correctOptionText: Increased capacitance and current leak mean less current reaches the next node, so it may fail to reach threshold

distractorRationale.a: Channel identity at the nodes is not the primary problem.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: without insulation, current dissipates across the membrane and the next node may not be depolarised to threshold.
distractorRationale.c: The resting potential is not what changes first.
distractorRationale.d: Pump function is not the mechanism of demyelinating conduction block.

questions.explanation: Demyelination exposes membrane with low Na+ channel density and removes insulation, so depolarising current leaks out and charges membrane capacitance. The depolarisation that reaches the next node can be sub-threshold, causing slowing or conduction block.

questions.stem: Compare impulse conduction in an unmyelinated axon and a myelinated axon. Include the effect of axon diameter and explain which fibre type is more energy-efficient.
markingGuide: Unmyelinated: continuous conduction, Na+ channels along the whole length, slow (about 0.5-2 m/s)
Myelinated: saltatory conduction, Na+ channels clustered at nodes of Ranvier, much faster
Myelin reduces capacitance and leak so current reaches the next node sooner
Larger diameter lowers internal resistance and increases speed in both types
Myelinated axons are more energy-efficient because less Na+ and K+ moves per impulse, so the pump has less to restore
questions.explanation: In unmyelinated axons every patch of membrane must be depolarised and recharged in turn, which is slow and ion-costly. Myelin insulates the internodes, so regenerative events happen only at nodes; this raises speed and lowers the ionic load the Na+/K+-ATPase must correct.
